In epispadias the meatus is on the dorsum with dorsal (upward) curvature, often with bladder exstrophy; hypospadias has a ventral meatus with ventral chordee.
Priapism is a persistent erection lasting more than 4 hours unrelated to sexual stimulation.
ADPKD has hepatic, pancreatic and arachnoid cysts with renal and extrarenal features, usually presents after 30, and progresses faster in men.
By the Weigert-Meyer rule the upper-moiety ureter opens inferomedially and tends to obstruct, while the lower-moiety ureter opens superolaterally and refluxes.
A ureterocoele, a cystic dilatation of the intravesical ureter, gives the cobra-head or spring-onion appearance on IVU.
Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty is the standard operation for pelviureteric junction obstruction.
ESWL is preferred for renal stones up to about 2 cm; larger stones are better treated with PCNL.
PCNL is indicated for stones over 2 cm, staghorn calculi and failed ESWL or RIRS; it is not first-line for all stones under 2 cm.
Collecting duct (Bellini) carcinoma is aggressive and carries the worst prognosis of the listed RCC types; chromophobe has the best.
Renal medullary carcinoma occurs almost exclusively in young people with sickle cell trait or disease.
The ureter narrows at the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the iliac vessels, and at its entry into the bladder; it does not cross the aorta.
Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer is treated by TURBT followed by intravesical mitomycin C or BCG according to risk.
Recurrent UTI is defined as two or more infections in 6 months or three or more in 12 months.
An isograft (syngeneic graft) is between genetically identical individuals such as identical twins.
Maastricht category III is controlled donation: cardiac arrest expected after planned withdrawal of life support.
Hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria and hyperuricosuria promote calcium oxalate stones; citrate inhibits stone formation, so hypocitraturia, not hypercitraturia, is the risk.
High-flow priapism from perineal trauma is painless arterial inflow; ischaemic priapism, for example from antipsychotics, is painful veno-occlusion needing urgent aspiration, so IV is false.
The classic triad of renal cell carcinoma is haematuria, flank pain and a palpable mass.
Early presentation, hypertension, male sex and PKD1 (not the milder PKD2) mutations predict faster progression to ESRD in ADPKD.
Indirect hernia lies lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, descends into the scrotum and is common in premature infants; on ring invagination its impulse hits the fingertip, not the pulp.
Femoral hernia is less common than inguinal hernia, even in women; the other statements about it are correct.
Ventral hernias are anterior abdominal wall hernias including spigelian, parastomal and lumbar; inguinal and femoral hernias are excluded.
SBP is ascitic fluid infection in cirrhosis diagnosed by neutrophils above 250/mm3 and treated with a third-generation cephalosporin; culture is often negative.
Chylolymphatic cysts are the commonest mesenteric cyst, have an independent blood supply and can be enucleated; they contain clear lymph, while enterogenous cysts contain turbid fluid.
A Plummer-Vinson web is lined by squamous mucosa on both surfaces; squamous above and columnar below describes a Schatzki ring.
GISTs are mesenchymal tumours with c-KIT mutations, size and mitotic index predict behaviour, and lymph node spread is rare.
Gastric outlet obstruction causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis with hyponatraemia and paradoxical aciduria; hyperkalaemia does not occur.
Anterior duodenal ulcers tend to perforate; posterior ulcers bleed by eroding the gastroduodenal artery, so statement C is wrong.
Acute liver failure is coagulopathy (INR above 1.5) with encephalopathy in a patient without prior liver disease and an illness of under 26 weeks.
Pain, ascites and hepatomegaly in a young woman with a thrombophilia and caudate lobe hypertrophy indicate hepatic venous outflow obstruction, which is Budd-Chiari syndrome.
Focal nodular hyperplasia with central scar and Kupffer cells has no malignant potential, so asymptomatic lesions need no treatment.
About 75 to 80% of liver blood flow comes from the portal vein and 20 to 25% from the hepatic artery.
Post-splenectomy sepsis is due mainly to encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae; Pseudomonas is not typical.
After emergency splenectomy, vaccines against encapsulated organisms are given once the patient recovers, before discharge.
Smoking, chronic pancreatitis and diabetes are risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which is slightly more common in men.
A pseudocyst is walled by fibrous or granulation tissue without an epithelial lining; intervention waits for the wall to mature and cystogastrostomy is an option.
Ranson admission criteria include age over 55, glucose over 200 mg/dL and WBC over 16,000; calcium is a 48-hour criterion. Statements 3 and 4 are merged in the stem.
Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum left from the vitellointestinal duct, lies on the antimesenteric border of the ileum and may contain gastric or pancreatic mucosa.
Ogilvie syndrome is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction with no mechanical cause; it shows marked caecal dilatation, risks caecal perforation and responds to IV neostigmine.
Crohn disease shows skip lesions, cobblestone mucosa and creeping fat; continuous mucosal involvement is a feature of ulcerative colitis.
Third-degree haemorrhoids prolapse and need manual reduction; only fourth-degree piles are permanently prolapsed. Banding suits first- and second-degree piles.
Sudden painless dark red rectal bleeding with pallor in a toddler under 2 and a soft abdomen without a mass suggests a bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa.
Peutz-Jeghers is autosomal dominant with STK11 mutation on chromosome 19 and mucocutaneous melanosis; polyps are hamartomatous, mainly small bowel.
Invasion into subserosa without breaching visceral peritoneum is T3, and 4 to 6 positive nodes is N2a, with no metastasis M0.
Amsterdam II requires three relatives, two successive generations and one diagnosis before 50, with FAP excluded, not confirmed.
Pseudocyst fluid is high in amylase and low in CEA, and its cytology shows inflammatory cells, not malignant ones; CEA above about 400 ng/mL suggests a mucinous neoplasm.
In cystic fibrosis the islets are initially spared and CF-related diabetes appears later in life; the CFTR gene is on chromosome 7 and male infertility is due to absent vasa.
Bartholin's (greater vestibular) gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch, close to the posterior end of the vestibular bulb.
The Bartholin's duct opens into the vestibule outside the hymen, at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third, in the groove between hymen and labium minus.
The Bartholin's duct is lined mainly by columnar/transitional epithelium, squamous only near its opening, so III is false; the gland is the female homologue of the bulbourethral gland.
Doderlein's bacillus (lactobacillus) is a Gram-positive rod that converts glycogen in vaginal cells to lactic acid, keeping the vaginal pH acidic.
Lactobacilli appear soon after birth under maternal estrogen, vanish within about two weeks, return at puberty and decline after menopause; all four statements are correct.
At surgery the ureter is identified as a pale glistening tube with longitudinal surface vessels that shows peristalsis when stroked.
In hysterectomy the ureter is at risk at the infundibulopelvic ligament, beside the cervix when clamping the cardinal ligament, and at the vaginal angles; round ligament division is safe.
The pelvic ureter is relatively narrowed at the pelvic brim, where the uterine artery crosses it and in its intravesical course; the sacroiliac joint is not a constriction site.
Levator ani has many slow-twitch fibres for sustained tonic support of pelvic organs, which explains its fatigue resistance.
The broad ligament contains the tube, uterine and ovarian vessels and Wolffian remnants such as Gartner's duct; the presacral plexus lies retroperitoneally over the sacral promontory.
The broad ligament is described as comprising the infundibulopelvic ligament laterally, the mesosalpinx, mesovarium and mesometrium.
The myometrium has both adrenergic (alpha and beta) and cholinergic receptors, so III is false; beta-agonists like isoxsuprine relax it and presacral neurectomy treats intractable dysmenorrhoea.
Level II (attachment) defects of the mid-vagina cause paravaginal defects, cystocele and stress incontinence; vault prolapse is a Level I (suspension) defect.
The paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts form the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina.
Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea and a tense bluish bulging membrane at the introitus is haematocolpos from an imperforate hymen.
Hysteroscopic septal resection (metroplasty) is the treatment of choice for a septate uterus with reproductive failure.

McCune-Albright syndrome combines peripheral precocious puberty, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and cafe-au-lait spots from an activating GNAS (Gs alpha) mutation; 'G3' appears to be a misprint for Gs.
Anovulatory cycles of the immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis are the commonest cause of puberty menorrhagia; coagulation disorders are the main organic cause to exclude.
Tanner stage II marks breast budding and sparse pubic hair, and thelarche is the first sign of puberty; both are true but R restates rather than explains A.
At menopause FSH rises above 40 mIU/mL, estradiol falls below 20 pg/mL and vaginal pH rises as lactobacilli disappear; adrenal DHEAS declines with age rather than increasing.
Hormone therapy relieves vasomotor symptoms, raises bone density, lowers vertebral and hip fracture risk and was associated with lower colorectal cancer risk in large trials.
Breast cancer, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, prior venous thromboembolism and active liver disease are all contraindications to menopausal hormone therapy.
GnRH is a decapeptide released in pulses from the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus into the portal circulation.
Both statements are true; R mainly concerns pulsatile versus continuous dosing, so it is treated as not explaining why GnRH releases both FSH and LH, though some would choose A.
Serum AMH reflects the pool of growing follicles and is the main cycle-independent marker of ovarian reserve.
AMH above 2 ng/mL suggests good reserve, below 0.5 ng/mL poor reserve, and very low values predict menopause within a few years, accompanied by rising FSH.
Ovulation follows about 34-36 hours after LH surge onset and 10-16 hours after the LH peak, with the estradiol peak about a day before; the listed intervals match the classic sequence.
Subnuclear glycogen vacuoles in endometrial glands appear 36-48 hours after ovulation and are the earliest histological sign of progesterone action.
The secretory endometrium shows subnuclear vacuolation, tortuous corkscrew glands and coiled spiral arteries; abundant mitoses and straight glands belong to the proliferative phase.
Under high estrogen the cervical mucus is thin and watery, stretches more than 10 cm, ferns on drying and has parallel channels that aid sperm passage.
In pregnancy, progesterone dominance makes the vaginal smear almost all intermediate (navicular) cells, giving a maturation index of about 0/95/5.
The LH surge triggers resumption and completion of meiosis I with extrusion of the first polar body just before ovulation, and starts luteinization of granulosa cells.
The newborn vaginal epithelium shows a pregnancy-like maturation index because maternal estrogen, progesterone and corticoids crossed the placenta.
Cytology alone every 3 years is the standard recommendation for women aged 25-29 (newer schedules also allow primary HPV testing every 5 years).
For women aged 30-65 with normal results, co-testing with cytology and high-risk HPV every 5 years is the preferred interval.
Screening stops after total hysterectomy for benign disease and after 65 with adequate negative screening; it continues after subtotal hysterectomy and for 20 years after CIN 2/3.
Endometrial sampling is indicated for suspected genital tuberculosis and for postmenopausal or abnormal perimenopausal bleeding, but it is not a routine test in every infertile woman.
In haematocolpos the distended vagina pushes the bladder up and elongates and stretches the urethra, causing acute retention.
AMH comes from granulosa cells of small antral follicles, which are increased in PCOS, so serum AMH is raised.
In Tanner stage V the areola recedes to the general breast contour and adult pubic hair extends onto the medial thighs.
Progesterone in the luteal phase gives clumped intermediate navicular cells on a dirty background of leukocytes and bacilli; cornified superficial cells on a clean smear are estrogenic.
Estrogen loss after menopause removes epithelial glycogen, so lactobacilli and lactic acid disappear and the vaginal pH rises.
Gravidity and parity count pregnancies, not fetuses, so a first pregnancy ending in twins is gravida 1, para 1.
Two abortions, one delivery and the current pregnancy make her gravida 4, and only the viable birth counts toward parity, so para 1.
Gravida counts all pregnancies, P2+1 means two births and one abortion, and grand multiparity begins at four or more births; recommended birth spacing figures vary between 2 and 3 years.
A daily fetal movement count is abnormal when it falls below 10 kicks in 12 hours or below 3 kicks an hour.
A reactive NST reliably predicts fetal wellbeing (very low false negative), while a non-reactive one often occurs in healthy fetuses; R is true but its link to A is debatable.
Modified BPP is NST plus AFI, abnormal with AFI below 5, so A and C are wrong; the low-score link to acidaemia actually belongs to the full biophysical profile.
The first-trimester combined test uses free beta-hCG, PAPP-A and nuchal translucency; MSAFP belongs to second-trimester screening.
CVS at 10-13 weeks has accuracy and loss rates comparable to amniocentesis, and limb defects are mainly linked to CVS before 9-10 weeks; the safety of late CVS only partly rests on R.
The first stage of labour runs from the onset of true labour pains to full cervical dilatation.
AMTSL is a uterotonic (oxytocin 10 IU IM) within a minute of birth, controlled cord traction, delayed cord clamping and uterine tone checks; in twins oxytocin waits for the last baby.
Early clamping in Rh isoimmunisation limits transfer of maternal antibodies and red cells to the baby; less neonatal jaundice is a related but separate effect.
Vaginal examination in labour confirms onset and presentation, assesses progress about every 4 hours and excludes cord prolapse after membranes rupture; stretching the vagina is not an indication.
Uncomplicated pregnancies may fly up to about 36 weeks; placenta praevia, pre-eclampsia and severe anaemia are contraindications.
Hypercoagulability persists into the early puerperium while fibrinolytic activity rises in the first days after delivery; the rise in fibrinolysis does not explain the persistence.
Maternal beta-blockers, methyldopa and opioids like pethidine can slow the fetal heart, whereas beta-agonist tocolytics such as ritodrine cause fetal tachycardia.
Fetal scalp blood sampling is contraindicated with maternal blood-borne infection such as HIV, fetal bleeding disorders and prematurity under 34 weeks; an abnormal CTG is its indication.
Early decelerations mirror contractions and come from vagal reflexes triggered by fetal head compression, so they are benign.
Late decelerations reflect uteroplacental insufficiency from placental disease, uterine hyperstimulation or oxytocin excess; cord compression gives variable decelerations.
Alpha-fetoprotein is made first by the yolk sac and then mainly by the fetal liver (with some from the fetal gut), not by the fetal kidneys or the maternal liver.
WHO 2018 intrapartum care recommends encouraging the birth position of the woman's choice, including upright positions, whether or not she has epidural analgesia.
A single deepest vertical pocket above 2 cm is normal, and falling liquor can reflect placental insufficiency with fetal hypoxia; R does not explain the cut-off.
Most miscarriages occur early, mostly before 12 weeks; autosomal trisomy is the commonest class of karyotype abnormality and monosomy X (45,X) the commonest single one.
Slight bleeding with a closed os, uterine size matching dates and fetal cardiac activity on ultrasound is a threatened miscarriage.
In septic abortion a temperature below 36 C signals endotoxic or septic shock and severe systemic infection rather than the usual febrile response.
Under the MTP rules a doctor qualifies by six months of OBG house job or assisting in 25 MTPs; a minor needs written guardian consent, and a husband's consent is never required.
Pregnancy in a girl under 18 is a sexual offence under POCSO with mandatory reporting, so the doctor must inform the police and register an MLC whatever the family wishes.
In ruptured ectopic pregnancy with shock, bleeding stops only at surgery, so resuscitation and laparotomy proceed together rather than one after the other.
The classical transvaginal discriminatory zone is a beta-hCG of about 1500 mIU/mL (newer guidance uses higher cut-offs up to 3500 before excluding intrauterine pregnancy).
Cervical pregnancy shows an empty uterine cavity, a barrel-shaped cervix and a gestational sac below the internal os; the twin peak sign marks dichorionic twins.
A caesarean scar pregnancy is implantation into the myometrial defect (niche) at the site of a previous caesarean scar.
Complete mole classically gives a uterus larger than dates, hCG above 100,000 mIU/mL, pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks and theca lutein cysts larger than 6 cm.
An IUD is avoided after molar evacuation until hCG normalises, because it may cause bleeding that mimics persistent trophoblastic disease and risks perforation.
Poor-prognosis GTN features include duration over 4 months, pretreatment hCG over 40,000, brain or liver metastases and a high WHO/FIGO score (7 or more).
Hydropic swelling of chorionic villi forms grape-like vesicles, and their passage per vaginam is diagnostic of a vesicular mole.
Fetus papyraceus is an early-dead twin that becomes flattened and mummified between the membranes of the live twin and the uterine wall.
TTTS needs a shared monochorionic placenta with vascular anastomoses, so it occurs only in monozygotic (monochorionic) twins, in about 10-15% of them.
The recipient twin becomes hypervolaemic, with polyhydramnios, polycythaemia, hypertension and possible cardiac failure; the donor is anaemic with oligohydramnios.
TTTS treatments include fetoscopic laser ablation of anastomoses (the treatment of choice), serial amnioreduction, septostomy and selective reduction.
In ascites floating bowel gives midline resonance with shifting dullness in the flanks, whereas a polyhydramniotic uterus is dull in the midline.
In circumvallate placenta the chorionic plate is smaller than the basal plate with a folded raised ring; placenta marginata is a different, flat-ring variant, so R does not explain A.
In TRAP sequence a normal pump twin perfuses an acardiac twin in reverse through large arterio-arterial and veno-venous anastomoses in a monochorionic placenta.
Left lateral rest relieves caval compression, improving venous return, cardiac output and renal and uteroplacental flow, which helps lower blood pressure.
Traditional teaching admits every established pre-eclampsia for close maternal and fetal monitoring, though current guidelines allow outpatient care without severe features.

Statement III is truncated and statement IV is missing, so the options cannot be checked; HELLP criteria are haemolysis on smear, raised AST/ALT and LDH, platelets under 100,000 and bilirubin over 1.2 mg/dL.
Gestational hypertension is BP of 140/90 or more on two readings 4 hours apart after 20 weeks or in the first 48 hours postpartum, without proteinuria, settling within 12 weeks.
Antenatal betamethasone or dexamethasone before 34 weeks speeds surfactant production and reduces neonatal RDS, which is why it is given in severe pre-eclampsia.
Antenatal steroids are routinely given below 34 weeks, so dexamethasone at 35 weeks is the incorrect step; some guidelines now allow late-preterm steroids.
Episiotomy is a planned incision of the perineum and posterior vaginal wall in the second stage of labour to enlarge the outlet.
Episiotomy is cut during a contraction once the perineum bulges and thins just before crowning, with about 3-4 cm of head visible.
Before forceps or ventouse the head must be engaged, the cervix fully dilated, the membranes ruptured and the bladder emptied.
External cephalic version turns a breech or transverse lie to cephalic before labour; a second twin in transverse lie is usually managed by internal podalic version.
Perforation by a suction cannula risks bowel and omental injury, so it needs laparoscopy or laparotomy to inspect the abdomen, unlike a small sound perforation.
Painless recurrent bright red bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus and a high floating head is typical of placenta praevia.
In concealed abruption blood collects behind the placenta, giving shock out of proportion to visible loss, a woody hard tender uterus and often fetal death.

Warfarin is teratogenic at 6-12 weeks, so heparin replaces it in the first trimester; current guidance uses therapeutic-dose heparin (and may allow low-dose warfarin), and option D contains stray audit text.
In asthma, bronchoconstricting PGF2-alpha (carboprost), ergometrine and the non-selective beta-blocker labetalol are avoided, while PGE1 (misoprostol) is safe.
Red degeneration of a fibroid in pregnancy is self-limiting and is treated conservatively with rest, analgesics and antibiotic cover; myomectomy in pregnancy is avoided.
Cytotoxics like cyclophosphamide and iodine-rich amiodarone are contraindicated in breastfeeding, while propylthiouracil and heparin are compatible.
A trial of labour is reasonable when the placental edge is more than 2 cm from the internal os on transvaginal scan; within 2 cm caesarean is preferred.
Some external bleeding together with a tense rigid tender uterus and continuous pain indicates partly revealed, partly concealed (mixed) abruption, often with hypertension.
Chloroquine prophylaxis in pregnancy is 300 mg base once weekly, though chloroquine resistance now limits its use in many areas.
Couvelaire uterus is extravasation of blood into the myometrium seen as a bluish, mottled uterus, so it is diagnosed only at laparotomy.
Antiphospholipid antibodies, including lupus anticoagulant, cause miscarriage and venous thrombosis in SLE; option D contains stray audit-log text.
Cholestasis with raised bile acids and transaminases was traditionally delivered at 37 weeks; newer guidance times delivery by bile acid level (38-39 weeks for 40-99 micromol/L).
Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended in pregnancy and lactation; live vaccines are avoided for theoretical fetal risk, which does not explain why the inactivated vaccine is safe.
Hydralazine, labetalol and, for refractory cases, nitroprusside are used for severe hypertension in pregnancy, while ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic and contraindicated.
Pudendal block gives perineal anaesthesia for outlet or low forceps and assisted vaginal breech delivery.
Type II posterior praevia is the dangerous mild type because the descending head compresses the placenta and cord against the sacral promontory, risking fetal hypoxia.
After a previous neural tube defect, 4 mg folic acid daily starts at least one month before conception and continues to 12 weeks, since the neural tube closes by day 28.
Megaloblastic anaemia in pregnancy is almost always from folate deficiency due to increased demand; B12 deficiency is rare.
Hydroxyurea is teratogenic and is stopped before conception, so A is false, while it does reduce painful vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease.
Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, speeding estrogen and progestogen metabolism and causing pill failure, so barrier methods or an IUD are preferred.
Severe (cerebral) falciparum malaria in any trimester is treated with IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then daily.
A soft relaxed uterus in placenta praevia and a tense tender uterus in abruption are both true, but the abruption finding does not explain the praevia finding.
Preterm labour is labour after viability but before 37 completed weeks (259 days) of gestation.
After a previous caesarean, pain between contractions, scar tenderness, haematuria and fetal heart abnormalities in labour indicate scar rupture.
A positive ICT means she is already sensitised, so anti-D is useless; titres are followed, with MCA Doppler or invasive testing once the critical titre is reached.

High pelvic inclination is usually listed as favouring occipitoposterior position with android/anthropoid pelvis, anterior placenta and brachycephaly, making all four true with no matching option; the embedded explanation contradicts itself.
A deflexed head in occiput posterior presents the occipitofrontal diameter (11.5 cm) instead of the suboccipitobregmatic (9.5 cm), so R explains A. The stem prints its own explanation.
In deep transverse arrest the head is engaged and deep in the pelvis with the sagittal suture in the transverse bispinous diameter and the anterior fontanel felt; it is not at the inlet.
Complete flexed breech, a non-engaged breech and adequate liquor favour version; extended legs splint the fetus and are a classic cause of failed ECV.
Multiple pregnancy, more than one previous caesarean and severe oligohydramnios contraindicate ECV; a reactive NST is reassuring, not a contraindication.
Average fetal weight, a flexed head and a Zatuchni-Andros score of 4 or more favour vaginal breech delivery; footling breech carries a high cord prolapse risk and favours caesarean.
Burns-Marshall delivers the after-coming head and Lovset's manoeuvre frees extended arms; both are true but they are separate manoeuvres, so R does not explain A.
The three types of abnormal cord descent are occult prolapse, cord presentation (membranes intact) and cord prolapse (membranes ruptured); entanglement is a separate entity.
Malpresentation, contracted pelvis, prematurity and procedures such as stabilising induction all leave space around the presenting part and predispose to cord prolapse.
Positioning (knee-chest/Trendelenburg), manual elevation of the presenting part and bladder filling relieve cord compression; pushing the cord back into the uterus is not recommended.
Secondary arrest is no cervical change for 2 hours or more in an active phase that had progressed normally, and it is usually due to malposition or cephalopelvic disproportion.
Macrosomia, maternal diabetes, a previous shoulder dystocia and anencephaly (small head relative to the shoulders) are all listed risk factors.

Shoulder dystocia cannot be reliably predicted; the turtle sign is typical and fundal pressure must be avoided. Statement III, that episiotomy is always given, is debatable, but B is the only option leaving out I.

On vaginal examination a hydrocephalic head shows wide sutures and fontanels and a crackling feel; a high head that cannot be pushed down is an abdominal finding, and the presenting diameter is larger.
Ultrasound in hydrocephalus shows a globular skull, wide sutures and fontanels, and dilated ventricles with a thin cortex; the vault bones are thinner than normal, not thicker.

4 mg folic acid from before conception to 12 weeks is the high-risk recommendation (400 mcg for others), and the neural tube closes about 28 days after conception, so periconceptional dosing is needed.
Amniotic fluid gives ferning and turns nitrazine paper blue; vaginal pH in pregnancy is acidic (4.5-5.5), while liquor is alkaline (7.0-7.5), so statement IV is false.
An abnormal fetal heart pattern, mostly prolonged or late decelerations, is the most consistent early sign of scar rupture and reflects loss of uteroplacental perfusion.
A short interpregnancy interval, high-dose oxytocin, a single-layer closure and a previous classical incision all increase the risk of scar rupture.
Anti-c and anti-Kell are the main non-D antibodies causing severe fetal haemolysis. Anti-Duffy and anti-Kidd can also cause HDFN, usually mild, so the wording is open to argument.
Cord bilirubin above about 4-5 mg/dL suggests exchange transfusion, and unconjugated bilirubin near 20 mg/dL crosses the blood-brain barrier causing kernicterus; conjugated bilirubin does not.
NEC and portal vein thrombosis with extrahepatic portal hypertension are late complications of exchange transfusion; hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia are immediate ones.

In a constriction ring the fetal heart is usually present and the mother is little affected, and the uterus does not rupture; the reason describes mechanics rather than explaining A, so B is intended.
A pathological retraction ring in obstructed labour is felt as an oblique abdominal groove with taut round ligaments and a tense, tender uterus; incoordinate action causes a constriction ring.
Under fundal dominance, waves start at cornual pacemakers and spread downward, and both their intensity and duration decrease away from the pacemaker.
Accepted thresholds are below 1-1.2 cm/hr in primigravidae and 1.5 cm/hr in multiparae; on the partograph, crossing the alert line is abnormal and crossing the action line calls for intervention.
Inadequate uterine activity dominates dysfunctional labour in nulliparae and disproportion or malposition in multiparae; these are parallel facts, so R does not explain A.
Cardiac failure, air embolism and metabolic upsets such as hypocalcaemia and hypoglycaemia occur during or right after exchange transfusion; NEC is delayed.
Extended legs, a short cord, obesity or tense abdominal muscles, and uterine anomalies all restrict fetal turning and cause failed external version.
An unsensitised Rh-negative mother of an Rh-positive baby gets 300 mcg anti-D IM within 72 hours of delivery, uncomplicated or not; 50 mcg is the first-trimester dose.

X-ray signs of IUFD are Spalding sign (about 7 days after death), Robert's sign of gas in the heart and great vessels (from about 12 hours) and spinal hyperflexion; cranial collapse is not seen within 12 hours.
Maceration after fetal death starts with skin blistering and peeling within about 12-24 hours, caused by aseptic autolysis once the circulation stops, so R explains A.
Prior preterm birth, genital tract infection and multiple pregnancy are clinical predictors; cervicovaginal fetal fibronectin is a biochemical marker.
Hydrops from Rh disease features maternal anti-D antibodies, polyhydramnios and the Buddha posture with a scalp-oedema halo; the placenta is large, pale and oedematous, not small and firm.
The osteomalacic pelvis, from calcium and vitamin D deficiency, is severely deformed with a triradiate inlet; a reniform inlet belongs to the rachitic flat pelvis.

The cord is not pushed back into the uterus but is placed in the vagina to limit vasospasm from cold and handling; the intended answer treats these as separate steps, though R could be read as related to A.
Cervicovaginal fetal fibronectin above 50 ng/mL between 24 and 34 weeks is the established biochemical predictor of preterm labour; its main value is a high negative predictive value.

In Rh haemolytic disease, bilirubin rising faster than 1 mg/dL per hour despite phototherapy calls for exchange transfusion; the cord thresholds offered (bilirubin >2, Hb <14) are not the standard values (>4-5, <11).
Hyperhomocysteinaemia gets folic acid, but a pregnant woman with previous thrombosis needs anticoagulant prophylaxis with heparin; warfarin is avoided in pregnancy.
Deep transverse arrest with a big baby or an inadequate pelvis is managed by caesarean section; rotational vaginal delivery is reserved for an adequate pelvis and an average-sized baby.
Secondary arrest of dilatation is classically defined as no cervical change for 2 hours or more in an active phase that had started normally.
A globular skull, wide sutures and dilated lateral ventricles with a high, unengaged head are the features of fetal hydrocephalus.
The four Ts of postpartum haemorrhage are tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin (coagulopathy), so all four listed causes apply.
A placenta not expelled 30 minutes after birth is retained; with a relaxed uterus and no bleeding the usual cause is a non-separated placenta from uterine atony.
In morbidly adherent placenta the villi attach directly to myometrium because decidua basalis and Nitabuch's layer are deficient, and ultrasound shows loss of the hypoechoic retroplacental zone.
In the obstetric anal sphincter injury classification, a 3a tear involves less than 50% of the external sphincter, 3b more than 50%, and 3c the internal sphincter too.
Severe perineal pain, tenesmus, urinary retention and a tense, tender, purple vulval swelling shortly after delivery are classic for an infralevator (vulval) haematoma.

A supralevator haematoma is rarer than an infralevator one and presents with unexplained shock and a mass above the inguinal ligament that pushes the uterus aside; the explanation is printed as statements 4-5.
Repeated vaginal examinations, prolonged membrane rupture, caesarean delivery and retained products all predispose to puerperal sepsis.
Group A and group B streptococci, E. coli and Bacteroides are all recognised causes of puerperal sepsis, and E. coli is among the commonest aerobes, so no option is a non-causative organism.
Treating cracked nipples means correcting the latch, giving antifungal treatment to mother and baby if there is thrush, and using lanolin or expressed milk on the nipple.
Puerperal mastitis is usually staphylococcal, and the organisms come from the infant's nose and throat and enter through cracked nipples.
Low first-trimester PAPP-A, abnormal uterine artery Doppler with notching in mid-pregnancy, and fetal echogenic bowel are all associated with later growth restriction.
Average blood loss is about 500 mL at vaginal delivery and about 1000 mL at caesarean section.
Rule of 30: systolic pressure down 30 mm Hg, heart rate up 30, respiratory rate above 30, haematocrit down 30% or urine below 30 mL/h means about 30% blood volume lost.
Unexplained shock with a mass above the inguinal ligament pushing the uterus to the other side indicates a supralevator (broad ligament) haematoma.
Puerperal pyrexia is an oral temperature of 100.4 F or more on two occasions 24 hours apart within the first 10 days, excluding the first 24 hours.
Dry wrinkled skin, a scaphoid abdomen, a thin cord, scant meconium-stained vernix and the 'old man look' describe a growth-restricted infant.
In asymmetric FGR, length and head growth are relatively spared while weight falls well below the centile minimum (about 600 g), so the head looks large for the body.
Brain sparing in asymmetric FGR keeps head growth while the liver and abdominal circumference fall behind, so the HC/AC ratio rises.
Brain-sparing redistribution reduces renal perfusion and often causes oligohydramnios, but it is not always present, so Statement-1 is false and Statement-2 is true.
A baby born before 37 completed weeks of gestation is preterm; low birth weight (under 2500 g) and small for gestational age are defined by weight, not by gestation.
Not breastfeeding raises the risk of SIDS, type 1 diabetes and obesity and is linked to lower IQ, so only the increased SIDS risk is a correct long-term risk.
The commonest cause of a retained, non-separated placenta is uterine atony; morbid adherence is a less common cause.

On MRI, placenta accreta spectrum shows dark intraplacental bands on T2-weighted images with abnormal vessels and uterine bulging; loss of the hypoechoic zone and Doppler hypervascularity are ultrasound signs.
A fresh perineal tear is repaired right after the placenta is delivered; if more than 24 hours late, repair is deferred and a complete tear is repaired after about 3 months.
A 3c tear involves both the external and internal anal sphincters; a fourth-degree tear also involves the anal epithelium.
A cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal bleeding between pericranium and skull bone, so it stops at the suture lines, unlike caput or subgaleal haemorrhage.
Postpartum depression is treated with psychotherapy and SSRIs such as fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline; reassurance alone suits postpartum blues.
Congenital CMV, rubella and toxoplasmosis are classic infectious causes of symmetric FGR; HPV does not cause FGR.
The partograph records the liquor (colour), the frequency and duration of contractions, and cervical dilatation, along with descent and maternal and fetal parameters.
In the modified WHO partograph the active phase starts at 4 cm and the alert line runs from 4 cm at 1 cm/hr; newer labour care guides use 5 cm.
Ovulation can return about 4 weeks after delivery in non-lactating women, so contraception should start by the third postpartum week.
Postpartum blues begin around day 3-5, affect roughly half of mothers, resolve within days and need only reassurance and support.
A healthy term infant needs about 100-110 kcal/kg/day (with about 150 mL/kg/day of milk).
Chromosomal abnormalities, structural fetal anomalies and placental or cord problems such as velamentous insertion all cause FGR.
A growth-restricted fetus with stable surveillance is generally delivered between 34 and 37 weeks, earlier if Doppler or CTG worsens.
A single palmar crease, brachycephaly, protruding tongue and congenital heart disease (often AV septal defect) point to trisomy 21.
E. coli is one of the commonest aerobic gram-negative causes of puerperal sepsis, together with group A and group B streptococci and anaerobes such as Bacteroides, so all four are responsible.
A tear of more than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness is 3b; anal epithelium involvement is fourth degree and EAS plus IAS is 3c.
A bulging anterior fontanelle, separated sutures and dilated scalp veins in a neonate show raised intracranial pressure; dehydration gives a sunken fontanelle.
Formula feeding is associated with more childhood obesity, more atopic dermatitis and diabetes, and lower IQ, so increased childhood obesity is the only correct option.
Fetal growth restriction (or SGA) is usually defined as weight below the 10th centile for gestational age.
Low first-trimester PAPP-A, abnormal uterine artery Doppler with notching at 20-24 weeks and echogenic bowel predict FGR; high beta-hCG is not a standard predictor.
In the WHO partograph the action line runs parallel to the alert line, 4 hours to its right.
Kernicterus comes from free unconjugated bilirubin crossing into the basal ganglia; in term infants the critical level is above about 20 mg/dL.
Short-lived tearfulness, anxiety and insomnia starting 3-5 days after delivery, without psychotic features, are postpartum (maternity) blues.
Supportive criteria for PID include fever above 38.3 C, mucopurulent discharge, WBCs on saline microscopy, and raised ESR or CRP.
Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing PID because it shows the inflamed tubes directly and allows samples to be taken for culture.
The fallopian tubes are involved in nearly all cases of female genital tuberculosis, usually on both sides, followed by the endometrium.
Genital tuberculosis is secondary, mostly from a pulmonary focus, and spreads to the genital tract mainly through the blood.
A tubercular granuloma has epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells and central caseation; safety-pin Donovan bodies belong to granuloma inguinale.
The cartridge-based NAAT (GeneXpert) detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance (rpoB mutations) in about 2 hours.
Rifampicin induces hepatic CYP450 and speeds up the metabolism of contraceptive steroids, so COCs become unreliable during anti-tubercular treatment.
The national daily regimen for new (drug-sensitive) TB is 2 months of HRZE followed by 4 months of HRE in the continuation phase.
Cervical tuberculosis can form a friable hypertrophic growth that mimics carcinoma; finding epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells points to granulomatous TB.
Sulfur granules (colonies of filamentous bacteria) are typical of actinomycosis, which is linked to long-term IUCD use and tubo-ovarian abscess.
MDR-TB means resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, with or without resistance to other drugs.
Pearl index = accidental pregnancies x 1200 / total months of exposure (patients observed x months of use), giving failures per 100 woman-years, not per 1000.
Ulipristal has antiglucocorticoid activity and is avoided in severe asthma treated with oral steroids; mifepristone has the same activity and is also cautioned, so the item is debatable.
Partial expulsion, active salpingitis and persistent heavy or irregular bleeding call for IUD removal; regular cyclical periods do not.
Enzyme inducers do not meaningfully reduce the efficacy of DMPA, which may also raise the seizure threshold, so it is preferred over COCs in women on antiepileptics.
An extended 84 active plus 7 inactive pill regimen gives one withdrawal bleed every 3 months, so 4 a year.
Vasectomy is simple and quick, needs backup contraception for about 3 months, and rarely recanalises; it does not increase testicular cancer risk.
Mala-N is a monophasic COC: every active tablet contains levonorgestrel 0.15 mg and ethinyl estradiol 30 mcg.
POPs suit lactating mothers because they do not reduce milk, but traditional POPs act mainly through thick cervical mucus and suppress ovulation in only about half of cycles.
A copper IUD inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse is the most effective emergency contraceptive (failure under 0.1%) and also gives ongoing contraception.
Genital warts from HPV 6 and 11 are usually multiple papillary lesions in cauliflower clusters, and pregnancy and discharge make them grow; a single flat lesion is atypical.
Painful, multiple, soft, purulent genital ulcers with gram-negative bacilli in a 'school of fish' pattern indicate chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
HIV is an RNA retrovirus that uses reverse transcriptase to make proviral DNA, so R is false; nucleic acid testing is the most sensitive and definitive diagnostic method.
Active primary genital herpes at term carries a high risk of neonatal infection, so caesarean delivery is recommended.
The progestogen-only pill does not reduce milk output and is the preferred oral method for breastfeeding women; oestrogen-containing pills are avoided before 6 months.
Sperm stored beyond the cut vas must be cleared, so backup contraception is used for about 3 months or 20 ejaculations until semen analysis shows azoospermia.
First-generation COCs contained 50 mcg or more ethinyl estradiol, but high-dose pills are not routinely given to teenagers; low-dose pills are preferred.
The contraceptive sponge must stay in for at least 6 hours after the last intercourse and no longer than about 24-30 hours in total.
Missing an inactive (placebo) pill does not affect protection; she discards it and carries on with the pack as usual.
A CD4 count below 200/microlitre (or below 14%) defines AIDS in an HIV-infected person, symptoms or not.
For type-specific HSV antibodies, the Western blot is the most specific serological test; PCR finds viral DNA, not antibodies.
Low-dose combined oral pills are the classic contraceptive of choice for a newly married couple who want to delay a first pregnancy: effective and quickly reversible.
Pills, patches and rings depend on the user, so typical-use failure is much higher than with IUDs and implants, and that is why non-LARC users have more unintended pregnancies.
Copper IUDs act through a spermicidal and inflammatory endometrial reaction that interferes enzymatically with implantation; thick cervical mucus and ovulation effects are hormonal (LNG) actions.
The diaphragm (with spermicide) can be inserted up to about 3 hours before coitus and must stay in place at least 6 hours after the last act.
Gossypol and GnRH analogues such as buserelin are experimental male contraceptives; the other options are female methods.
A painful, soft, purulent ulcer after a 3-5 day incubation with a unilateral suppurative bubo is typical of chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
Sperm stored distal to the cut vas take about 3 months or 20 ejaculations to clear, so backup contraception is needed; R explains A.
COCs roughly halve endometrial and ovarian cancer risk and lower colorectal cancer risk; they do not reduce breast cancer risk.
Progestogen-only pills do not suppress milk volume, which is why they are preferred in breastfeeding women; R explains A.
Painless rubbery inguinal nodes progressing to buboes are characteristic of lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by the L1-L3 serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis.
Unexplained genital bleeding, recent septic abortion and a distorted uterine cavity contraindicate IUCD insertion; nulliparity does not.
LNG-IUS acts mainly by endometrial suppression and thick cervical mucus, and ovulation usually continues, so A is false while R is true.
Traditional teaching advises continuing the pill with an added barrier method during broad-spectrum antibiotics; newer guidance says non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics need no backup.
Tobacco-pouch fimbrial ends, tubal diverticula and vascular or lymphatic intravasation of dye on HSG are classic for genital tuberculosis.
Candida causes intense itching with thick, white, curdy discharge; thin, greenish-yellow frothy discharge belongs to trichomoniasis, so R is false.
A painful, tender swelling in the posterior labium majus with fever and difficulty walking is a Bartholin abscess; a cyst is painless.
Cervical carcinoma, cervical polyp and chlamydial cervicitis bleed on contact; pelvic congestion causes congestive dysmenorrhoea, not contact bleeding.
In FIGO PALM-COEIN, PALM (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy) are the structural causes, diagnosed by imaging or histology, so A is false and R is true.
In second-degree uterine prolapse the external os protrudes outside the introitus while the uterine body stays inside the vagina.
A painless fluctuant swelling in the posterior labium majus that makes the vulval cleft S-shaped is a Bartholin cyst; marsupialization is the preferred treatment.
Letrozole, clomiphene and hCG (as the ovulation trigger) are used to induce ovulation; metformin only corrects insulin resistance.
Fecundability is the probability of achieving pregnancy in a single menstrual cycle.
Pelvic endometriosis distorts anatomy and causes dense adhesions around the ureter, so it carries the highest risk of ureteric injury at hysterectomy.
The Manchester (Fothergill) repair preserves the uterus, which is why it counts as conservative surgery for prolapse; R explains A.
Presacral neurectomy interrupts uterine sensory fibres and is a rarely used surgical option for refractory primary dysmenorrhoea.
In procidentia (third-degree prolapse) the whole uterus lies outside the introitus with complete eversion of the vagina.
Leydig failure lowers testosterone, and the loss of negative feedback raises LH; the high LH is a consequence of A, not its cause, so R does not strictly explain A.
The Fothergill operation conserves the uterus and suits younger women with prolapse who want to keep the uterus or their reproductive function.
Progesterone is thermogenic and stays high in pregnancy, so the luteal rise in basal body temperature is sustained; R explains A.
Fecundity is the probability of achieving a live birth within one cycle; fecundability refers to pregnancy.
Pills, patches and rings depend on correct daily or weekly use, so their typical-use failure rate is far higher than with LARC; R explains A.
Early menarche and PCOS raise fibroid risk and smoking lowers it, while multiparity is protective, not a risk factor.
Red degeneration is aseptic necrobiosis of vascular origin, typical of mid-pregnancy, with a raw-beef look; infection plays no part.
Submucous fibroids are the least common type (about 5%) but distort the cavity and cause the most bleeding, infertility and miscarriage. Interstitial and intramural mean the same thing.
Red degeneration has a fishy odour from fatty acids; the haemolysed blood explains the red colour, not the smell, so R is false.

Call-Exner bodies, small follicle-like rosettes of granulosa cells around eosinophilic material, are characteristic of granulosa cell tumour.
FIGO stage IIIC2 endometrial cancer means para-aortic nodal metastasis, with or without pelvic nodes; IIIC1 is pelvic nodes only.

Heavy menstrual bleeding with an enlarged 16-week uterus and a negative pregnancy test is most likely a uterine fibroid.
Functional cysts (follicular, luteal) are lined by the granulosa or luteinised cells of the follicle or corpus luteum they arise from.
Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma made mostly of thyroid tissue, which can occasionally cause hyperthyroidism.

Early first pregnancy, poor genital hygiene and multiple sexual partners raise CIN risk; vitamin A deficiency, not high intake, is the risk factor.

Submucous fibroids distort the cavity and enlarge the endometrial surface, causing the most bleeding and reproductive symptoms; R explains A.
Meigs syndrome is ascites with a right-sided hydrothorax and an ovarian fibroma, resolving after the tumour is removed; a left-sided effusion is not typical.
Tumour 4 cm or larger, deep stromal invasion and circulating HPV mRNA worsen prognosis; squamous histology is not worse than adenocarcinoma.
Prophylactic oophorectomy is for high-risk women such as BRCA carriers, women with prior breast cancer and those over 45 having pelvic surgery; an enlarged ovary needs therapeutic surgery.
COCs, breastfeeding and tubal ligation lower ovarian cancer risk; fertility drugs are considered a possible risk factor.
Classic FIGO cervical staging relies on pelvic examination under anaesthesia, endocervical curettage and biopsy; ultrasound was not among the staging procedures.
After a molar pregnancy, age over 40, hCG above 100,000 IU/L and large theca lutein cysts over 6-8 cm predict progression to GTN.

Persistent GTN after evacuation shows irregular bleeding, subinvolution and persisting theca lutein cysts with plateauing or rising hCG, not a rapid fall.
Squamous metaplasia at the cervical transformation zone is most active in high-oestrogen states such as a first pregnancy and is driven by the acidic vaginal pH.

Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis independent of liver and kidney, so it is preferred in combined organ failure.
Prilocaine is metabolised to o-toluidine, which oxidises haemoglobin and causes methaemoglobinaemia.
Halothane hepatitis results from trifluoroacetylated metabolites provoking immune liver injury, which has limited its use.
Thiopentone lowers cerebral metabolic oxygen demand, cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, which is why it is used in neuroanaesthesia.
RSI uses an intravenous induction agent with a rapid-onset relaxant to secure the airway in emergency patients at aspiration risk, not an inhalational agent.
Bupivacaine's higher protein binding and lipid solubility give it a longer duration of action than lidocaine.
High-dose rocuronium has an onset close to suxamethonium and can be rapidly reversed by sugammadex, making it suitable for RSI.
ASA is a preoperative physical status grade, POSSUM and ACS NSQIP are risk prediction tools; Mallampati is an airway test, not a mortality score.

Hepatitis B vaccine prevents hepatocellular carcinoma and HPV vaccine prevents cervical and other HPV cancers.

Age, sex and genetic factors are non-modifiable risk factors for hypertension.

One-way communication is the didactic method and two-way communication, with feedback and discussion, is the Socratic method.
Health communication covers information, education, motivation, persuasion, counselling and organization; disease surveillance is not one of its functions.
Persuasion is a conscious attempt by one person to change another's beliefs, values or behaviour in a desired direction.

Health education encourages reflective thinking, appeals to reason and develops individuality, while propaganda discourages thinking, appeals to emotion and standardises attitudes; statement 3 is not the standard contrast.
The medical model sees health education as part of recognising and treating disease with medical technology.
In the motivation model people move from awareness to motivation and then to action. This is a simplified form of the adoption sequence, so the wording is loose.
The social intervention model takes a broad ecological view, looking at community health problems and their social and environmental solutions.
Credibility, moving from known to unknown, and feedback are principles of health education; participation must be voluntary, never enforced.
Role play, symposia and workshops are group-approach methods of health communication.
Radio, the internet and posters reach the public as mass media; home visits belong to the individual approach.
Personal contact, home visits and personal letters are individual-approach methods.
Propaganda offers ready-made ideas through emotional appeal and discourages independent thinking.
The communication process has sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback; legislation is not a component.
Adoption follows a sequence of awareness, interest, evaluation, trial or decision, and finally action.

Incineration is the method of choice for most hazardous healthcare waste, such as anatomical waste; recyclable plastics and sharps are not incinerated.
The yellow category takes anatomical waste, soiled waste and cytotoxic-contaminated items; IV tubing and catheters are red-category recyclable waste.
Microbiology, biotechnology and other clinical laboratory waste is yellow category; it is pre-treated and then incinerated.
Contaminated recyclable waste such as tubing, bottles, urine bags, syringes without needles and gloves goes in red bags.
Sharps, including needles and blades, go in a puncture-proof, leak-proof, tamper-proof white translucent container.
Blue cardboard boxes take contaminated glassware and metallic body implants. Syringes with fixed needles are white category and cytotoxic vials are yellow.
Cytotoxic drugs and items contaminated with them are yellow-category waste, sent for incineration.
Expired or discarded medicines, including antibiotics and cytotoxic drugs, are yellow-category pharmaceutical waste.
Chemical liquid waste such as X-ray developer and formalin is a yellow-category item, collected separately and treated before discharge.
Broken or contaminated glassware and non-cytotoxic vials and ampoules go in blue-marked puncture-proof boxes.
IV tubing with the needle removed is contaminated recyclable plastic, so it goes in the red bag.
Chlorinated plastics such as PVC tubing and blood bags give off dioxins and furans when burned, so they must not be incinerated.
Metallic body implants are collected with glassware in blue-marked puncture-proof cardboard boxes.
Needles and other sharps, including those from needle cutters, go in the white translucent puncture-proof container.
Items soiled with blood or body fluids, such as soiled linen and dressings, are yellow-category waste. Stem and option D contain long passages from another chapter.

The biomedical concept, rooted in germ theory, defines health as the absence of disease.
The ecological concept sees health as a dynamic equilibrium between man and environment kept up by continuous adaptation; the environment is not only physical.
The psychosocial concept holds that health is both a biological and a social phenomenon, shaped by social, psychological and cultural factors.
The holistic concept combines the biomedical, ecological and psychosocial concepts and stresses promoting and protecting health.
HDI uses life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and GNI per capita at PPP; the literacy rate was replaced in 2010.
PQLI combines infant mortality, life expectancy at age one and literacy on a 0 to 100 scale; it leaves out income, and HDI runs from 0 to 1.
The infant mortality rate is the most sensitive indicator of how available, used and effective health services are.
DALY measures disease burden as years of healthy life lost to premature death and disability.
DALY is the sum of years of life lost to premature death (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD).
GNP per capita, dependency ratio and family size are socioeconomic indicators; maternal mortality rate is a mortality indicator.
The submerged part of the iceberg is the hidden disease: latent, inapparent, presymptomatic and undiagnosed cases and carriers.
Primordial prevention stops risk factors from emerging in a population where they have not yet appeared.
Primary prevention lowers incidence, secondary prevention lowers prevalence and tertiary prevention limits disability; primordial prevention targets whole populations, not patients.
The WHO sequence runs from disease to impairment, then disability, then handicap.

In an average Indian diet protein gives 10 to 15%, fat 15 to 30% and carbohydrate 50 to 80% of energy; alcohol does not give 10 to 20% in most adults.
Essential amino acids cannot be made in adequate amounts and must come from the diet, and both kinds are needed for tissue protein; they also occur in plant proteins.
A biologically complete protein has every essential amino acid in the proportions humans need; most animal proteins qualify, most vegetable proteins do not.
Phenylalanine, valine and threonine are essential amino acids; glycine is non-essential.
Proteins build and repair tissue, maintain osmotic pressure and are used to make antibodies, enzymes and hormones; they supply energy only when calorie intake is inadequate.
Lysine and threonine are the limiting amino acids in cereals and methionine in pulses; animal proteins are complete.
Egg protein is the reference protein, animal proteins are complete, vegetable proteins are poorer in essential amino acids, and Indians get most of their protein from cereals and pulses.
Coconut and palm oils are exceptions among vegetable oils because they are very high in saturated fatty acids; the other three statements are correct.
Linoleic acid is the most important essential fatty acid, arachidonic and linolenic acids are also counted as essential, and deficiency causes phrenoderma (toad skin).
Partial hydrogenation produces trans fats, which raise LDL, lower HDL and are atherogenic; they take years, not days, to clear from the body.
Carbohydrates are the main energy source at 4 kcal per gram, are needed for complete fat oxidation and help make some non-essential amino acids; dietary fibre also includes lignin.
Night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots and keratomalacia are all eye signs of vitamin A deficiency.

K1 comes from green leafy vegetables and K2 from gut bacteria; long antibiotic courses cause deficiency, and newborns need prophylactic vitamin K.

In latent iron deficiency stores and ferritin are low, haemoglobin is still normal and transferrin saturation falls below 15%. That it is the most prevalent stage in India is not a standard fact.

NEERI Nagpur developed the Nalgonda technique: lime and alum are added in turn, then flocculation, sedimentation and filtration. It is used on groundwater too.

Parkinson's disease causes reduced blinking, drooling and hypophonia; handwriting becomes small (micrographia), not large.
Headache phase involves extracranial vasodilatation, common migraine is migraine without aura, and aura is most often visual; all three are correct.
Sleep deprivation, missed antiepileptic doses, recreational drugs and physical exhaustion are all recognised seizure triggers.
Hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency and thiamine deficiency are treatable causes of dementia; dementia with Lewy bodies is a progressive neurodegenerative disease.
Frontotemporal dementia causes personality change and language disturbance with early relative memory sparing; cholinesterase inhibitors are not effective.
The 4AT assesses Alertness, AMT4, Attention and Acute change or fluctuating course; apnoea is not a component.
Brain death requires irreversible coma, absent brainstem reflexes and apnoea despite raised PaCO2; hypothermia must be excluded, not present.

Familial Alzheimer's, Huntington's and Wilson's disease are inherited causes of dementia; punch-drunk syndrome results from repeated head trauma.
Cataract causes painless gradual visual loss in a white eye; keratitis, episcleritis and acute glaucoma all cause acute red eye.
Eyelid BCC is the commonest eyelid malignancy, rarely metastasises and extensive lesions need Mohs surgery; it is commoner on the lower lid.
Graves' ophthalmopathy is the commonest cause of adult proptosis, is a clinical diagnosis and flares on steroid withdrawal; proptosis is often asymmetric.

Alopecia areata, telogen effluvium and secondary syphilis cause non-scarring alopecia; cutaneous sarcoidosis typically causes scarring alopecia.
New vitiligo lesions at a site of trauma such as sunburn are the Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon.
Central facial erythema, telangiectasia and pustules without comedones in an adult over 30 is rosacea; acne vulgaris has comedones.
Sharply defined symmetrical depigmented patches enhanced by Wood's lamp in a patient with autoimmune thyroiditis is vitiligo.
Pseudo-Koebner phenomenon, from autoinoculation along trauma, occurs in viral warts and molluscum; psoriasis and lichen planus show true Koebner.
A delusion is a false, fixed belief not amenable to reason and out of keeping with the patient's cultural background.

Budd-Chiari is hepatic venous outflow obstruction linked to thrombophilias, presenting with pain and ascites, and mainly affects young women.

Peritoneal metastases most commonly appear as multiple discrete nodules from transcoelomic seeding.
Spigelian hernia is an interparietal hernia that tracks between the layers of the abdominal wall muscles.
Stoppa, Lichtenstein and laparoscopic TEP are mesh-based tension-free repairs; Desarda is a tissue repair.
Perianal disease is common in Crohn's disease; fistulae and strictures are features of Crohn's, and the rectum is often spared.
The Sengstaken-Blakemore tube provides balloon tamponade for bleeding oesophagogastric varices.

Amyloidosis and Gaucher's disease are metabolic or storage causes of splenomegaly.
Mesenteric cysts usually present as a painless periumbilical swelling, are commoner in women and adults, and are treated by excision.
Morgagni hernia is a congenital anterior defect between sternal and costal diaphragmatic slips, commonly containing transverse colon.
Late dumping is reactive hypoglycaemia in the second hour after a meal, lasting about 30-40 minutes with tremor and faintness; it is relieved by food, while lying down relieves early dumping.

Complete third nerve palsy causes ptosis, a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye from unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique.
Alopecia areata, telogen effluvium and secondary syphilis cause non-scarring hair loss; cutaneous sarcoidosis causes scarring alopecia.

Wolff's law states that bone remodels, depositing or resorbing, in response to the mechanical stresses placed on it.
