Levodopa best relieves bradykinesia and rigidity, not tremor; little reaches the brain, domperidone counters nausea and hallucinations can occur.
Sickle cell disease, smoking and atrial fibrillation raise stroke risk; raised, not low, fibrinogen is the risk factor.
Myasthenic weakness worsens with activity through the day, involves bulbar muscles and can be induced by penicillamine; the antibodies target post-junctional acetylcholine receptors.
TB meningitis is paucibacillary so CSF smears are often negative, culture remains the gold standard, and Xpert MTB/RIF (Ultra) is the recommended initial test.
Night paraesthesia and weak thumb abduction are typical and hypothenar wasting is ulnar; palm sensation is often spared via the palmar cutaneous branch, but A is the best code.
Graphesthesia and stereognosis test cortical (parietal) sensory integration, provided primary sensation is intact.
Tetracyclines, retinoids and excess vitamin A are the classic drug causes of idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Lower motor neuron lesions give fasciculations, hyporeflexia and no clonus, with a flexor or absent plantar response.
Increasing age is the single strongest risk factor for dementia.
Recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations are a core feature of dementia with Lewy bodies.
HIV, alcohol and phenytoin cause polyneuropathy; among antituberculars it is isoniazid, not rifampicin, that does.
ICH is about 10% of strokes and hypertensive bleeds arise from deep penetrating arteries (putamen, thalamus); cocaine and methamphetamine are major causes in the young.
Dominant parietal lesions cause dysphasia, acalculia and dyslexia; contralateral neglect results from non-dominant parietal lesions.
Axillary freckling and neurofibromas are NF1 features while cutaneous schwannomas belong to NF2, leaving the option without statement 3.
Parkinson disease shows bradykinesia, rigidity and a mask-like face; the gait is festinating, not spastic.
Carbamazepine is the first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia.
Constructional and visuospatial skills depend on the non-dominant parietal lobe, whose lesions cause constructional apraxia.
Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome causes upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation.
Cauda equina compression is a lower motor neuron lesion with back pain, areflexia and sphincter loss; an extensor plantar indicates an upper motor neuron lesion.
The Cushing triad is hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration; hypothermia is not part of it.
Thyroid dysfunction and hypercalcemic hyperparathyroidism are listed endocrine causes of delirium; hypoparathyroidism mainly causes tetany and seizures.
Amaurosis fugax comes from carotid emboli that lodge in the ophthalmic artery or its retinal branches; posterior cerebral artery lesions cause homonymous field defects.
The occipital pole representing the macula gets dual supply from MCA and PCA, so PCA infarcts may spare macular vision.
Horner syndrome causes partial ptosis, apparent enophthalmos, miosis and anhidrosis.
In adults the spinal cord ends at the L1-L2 level, not at L5; the other statements are correct.
Myotonic dystrophy characteristically causes distal weakness, whereas Duchenne, Becker and FSHD involve proximal muscles.
Huntington disease, Alzheimer disease and thiamine deficiency cause dementia; vitamin D toxicity is not a recognised cause.
A positive acetylcholine receptor antibody is virtually specific for myasthenia gravis and establishes the diagnosis.
Cerebrovascular disease is the commonest cause of new-onset seizures in the elderly.
Allodynia is pain from a normally innocuous stimulus; hyperalgesia is exaggerated pain from a painful stimulus.
Clonus with spasticity and hyperreflexia marks an upper motor neuron lesion; fasciculations, hyporeflexia and wasting are lower motor neuron signs.
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome results from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery or the vertebral artery.
Gowers sign reflects proximal pelvic girdle weakness and is classic in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Brain death requires absent brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, gag); spinal reflexes including plantar responses may persist and are not part of the criteria.
Poliovirus is a picornavirus, early cramps with fasciculations and CSF neutrophils occur; recent tonsillectomy increases, not reduces, bulbar polio risk.
Bartholin gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch, secretes alkaline mucus and is homologous to the bulbourethral gland; its duct is columnar-lined except near its opening.
The ureter is at risk at the infundibulopelvic ligament, beside the cervix when clamping the cardinal ligament and at the vaginal angles; round ligament division is far from it.
Hegar's sign: on bimanual examination at 6-10 weeks, the soft isthmus lets the abdominal and vaginal fingers be apposed below the uterine body.
In sickle cell pregnancy, hydroxyurea is stopped before conception, penicillin prophylaxis is given and unpressurised air travel is avoided; iron is given only for proven deficiency.
Ruptured membranes and a previous caesarean scar are classic contraindications to ECV, and dead fetus and obesity are also listed; whether all four count varies between sources.
Thalassemia trait shows low MCV and MCH with normal MCHC, raised HbA2 and normal or raised serum iron, unlike iron deficiency.
Hyperemesis can cause peripheral neuritis and Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency, Mallory-Weiss tears and coma; cardiac failure is not a recognised complication.
Occipitoposterior position is favoured by android or anthropoid pelvis, high pelvic inclination, anterior placenta and abnormal uterine contractions.
Polyhydramnios, twins, prematurity and stabilising induction (artificial rupture of membranes) all predispose to cord prolapse.
The 10-13 week scan in twins confirms the number of fetuses and their viability, sets chorionicity (lambda or T sign) and screens for major malformations.
Fetal breathing movements appear by about 11 weeks, surfactant around 24 weeks and insulin secretion after the first trimester; meconium is present by mid-gestation.
In pregnancy CRH, ACTH and aldosterone all rise, while maternal serum iodine falls due to increased renal clearance.
The suboccipitofrontal diameter (10 cm) engages with incomplete flexion; suboccipitobregmatic with full flexion and occipitofrontal with marked deflexion.
Normal pregnancy is diabetogenic: insulin resistance with higher insulin secretion gives fasting hypoglycaemia and postprandial hyperglycaemia.
The uterus is supplied mainly by the uterine arteries with anastomotic contributions from the ovarian and vaginal arteries.
The plane of least pelvic dimensions (ischial spines) is the narrowest plane, where internal rotation (not external) happens, the pelvic axis curves forward and the pudendal block is given.
Pregnancy raises cardiac output, stroke volume and heart rate while systemic vascular resistance falls.
The sagittal suture lies between the parietal bones; the coronal joins frontal and parietal bones and the posterior fontanelle is triangular.
hCG is a placental glycoprotein whose alpha subunit is shared with LH, FSH and TSH; levels are higher in multiple pregnancy.
Red degeneration occurs mainly in pregnancy and puerperium, shows a raw-beef cut surface and may partly recover (necrobiosis); its cause is vascular, not infective.
Hormone receptor positive endometrial cancers carry a better prognosis; grade 3, aneuploidy and HER-2/neu are adverse.
Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, headache and visual disturbance with prolactin above 100 ng/mL indicate a prolactinoma.
Primary dysmenorrhoea affects mainly adolescents, occurs only with ovulatory cycles, often improves after vaginal delivery and has no pelvic pathology.
In POP-Q the hymen is zero, points above it are negative and below it positive, and total vaginal length is measured with the prolapse reduced.
A cystocele is reducible, gives an impulse on coughing and admits a metal catheter into the swelling, unlike a Gartner cyst.
The current WHO lower reference limits are volume 1.4 mL, total motility 42%, progressive motility 30% and normal morphology 4%.
A simple VVF is small (up to about 2.5-3 cm), supratrigonal and not related to malignancy or prior radiation.
With dye in the bladder, a stained middle swab indicates a vesicovaginal fistula; a wet unstained upper swab suggests ureterovaginal fistula.
Postpartum psychosis begins suddenly, usually within the first few days after delivery; it is linked with a personal or family history, recurs in about 20-50%, and ECT is not first line in all cases.
Postpartum blues affect about half of mothers in the first week, have no specific endocrine abnormality and are managed with reassurance and support.
FGR is predicted by low first-trimester PAPP-A (not beta-hCG), abnormal uterine artery Doppler at 20-24 weeks, fetal echogenic bowel and maternal medical disorders.
Pathologically accreta shows absent decidua basalis and a deficient Nitabuch layer; loss of the retroplacental clear zone is an ultrasound sign, not a pathological finding.
The WHO partograph records time, temperature, pulse, BP and urine (volume, protein, acetone) but not maternal respiratory rate.
At 12 months a child says 1-2 meaningful words and plays simple ball games; a vocabulary of 8-10 words is expected around 18 months.
Ureteric narrowings are at the pelviureteric junction, the iliac artery crossing, the bladder wall entry and the orifice, not at the aorta.
Renal cell carcinoma (Grawitz tumour) may present with PUO and tumour thrombus embolism, but haematuria is absent in many patients.
The bladder is at risk in hysterectomy, rectal surgery and sliding inguinal hernia repair, but superficial inguinal node dissection does not approach it.
Ectopic ureters are more common in females, drain the upper pole of a duplex kidney and cause continuous incontinence in girls.
Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty repairs pelviureteric junction obstruction of the renal pelvis.
RCC arises from proximal tubular epithelium, has clear cell, papillary and chromophobe subtypes and is treated surgically when localised; it is commoner in men.
ADPKD has hepatic, pancreatic and arachnoid cysts, renal and extrarenal features and faster progression in men; it usually manifests after 30 years.
ESWL is mainly used to fragment renal and ureteric stones, usually under 2 cm.
Pseudotubercles are the earliest specific cystoscopic sign of urinary schistosomiasis, followed by nodules, sandy patches and ulcers.
Most hypospadias are distal, with the meatus at the coronal or subcoronal region just proximal to the glans.
Asthma control aims at night waking no more than twice a month, symptoms and reliever use no more than twice a week, and at most one exacerbation a year.
Silica, cadmium and coal dust are recognised occupational causes of COPD; asbestos mainly causes pleural disease, fibrosis and malignancy.
Chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus and immotile sperm form Kartagener syndrome, a primary ciliary dyskinesia.
Cystic fibrosis is confirmed by sweat chloride and CFTR genotyping, with faecal fat showing pancreatic insufficiency; lung biopsy has no diagnostic role.
CBNAAT detects rifampicin resistance, LPA detects INH and rifampicin resistance, LED fluorescence beats ZN; IGRA cannot diagnose active TB.
Isoniazid causes pyridoxine-deficiency peripheral neuropathy.
Ethambutol causes optic (retrobulbar) neuritis with red-green colour loss and must be stopped.
HPOA, SIADH, membranous nephropathy and gynaecomastia are all paraneoplastic, non-metastatic manifestations of lung cancer.
Thymoma, retrosternal goitre and germ cell tumours are anterior mediastinal; neurogenic tumours are posterior mediastinal.
Interstitial lung disease/fibrosis is usually taught as the commonest pulmonary manifestation of RA, though pleural involvement is common at autopsy.
Extensive sclerosis of chest wall skin in systemic sclerosis restricts chest movement, called hidebound chest.
Penicillin, sulfasalazine, methotrexate and beta-blockers such as nadolol are all listed causes of drug-induced pulmonary eosinophilia.
Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure.
The classic definition is mean PAP 25 mmHg or more at rest; the 2022 definition lowered the threshold to above 20 mmHg.
Phrenic palsy, subphrenic abscess and loss of lung volume after lobectomy raise a hemidiaphragm; pleural effusion does not truly elevate it.
Cheese washer's lung is due to Penicillium casei, with Aspergillus clavatus also listed as an antigen source.
Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is classic for silicosis.
Obesity, acromegaly, male sex and alcohol all predispose to obstructive sleep apnoea.
In the proliferative phase of ARDS type II pneumocytes proliferate and re-epithelialise the alveoli; hyaline membranes belong to the exudative phase.
Adequate PEEP prevents cyclic alveolar collapse and reopening, i.e. atelectrauma.
Indirect hernia is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, reaches the scrotum, is common in preterm infants; impulse at the fingertip, pulp impulse means direct.
Femoral hernia is less common than inguinal hernia, even in women.
Ventral hernias include spigelian, parastomal and lumbar hernias; inguinal and femoral hernias are excluded.
SBP is diagnosed by ascitic neutrophils above 250/mm3 and treated with a third-generation cephalosporin; culture is negative in up to 60%.
Chylolymphatic cysts are the commonest mesenteric cysts, have their own blood supply and can be enucleated; turbid fluid with bowel wall describes enterogenous cysts.
The lower oesophagus is supplied mainly by the left gastric artery, not the right gastric.
A Plummer-Vinson web is lined by squamous mucosa on both sides; squamous above and columnar below describes a Schatzki ring.
GISTs are c-kit-driven mesenchymal tumours with equal sex incidence; size and mitotic index predict behaviour, and nodal spread is rare.
Anterior duodenal ulcers perforate; posterior ulcers bleed by eroding the gastroduodenal artery.
Acute liver failure needs coagulopathy (INR above 1.5), encephalopathy, no prior liver disease and illness shorter than 26 weeks.
About 75-80% of hepatic blood flow comes from the portal vein and 20-25% from the hepatic artery.
OPSI is caused by encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae; Pseudomonas is not typical.
After emergency splenectomy, vaccines are given once the patient has recovered from surgery (about two weeks after) and before discharge.
Smoking, chronic pancreatitis and diabetes are risk factors for pancreatic adenocarcinoma; it is more common in men.
A pseudocyst has a wall of fibrous or granulation tissue with no epithelial lining, which is why it is called a pseudocyst.
Ranson criteria on admission include age over 55, WBC over 16,000 and glucose over 200 mg/dL; low calcium is a 48-hour criterion.
Meckel diverticulum is a true vitellointestinal duct remnant on the antimesenteric border of the ileum and may contain gastric or pancreatic mucosa.
Ogilvie syndrome is pseudo-obstruction with no mechanical cause; it shows caecal dilatation, risks caecal perforation and responds to IV neostigmine.
Crohn disease shows skip lesions, cobblestoning and creeping fat; continuous mucosal involvement is typical of ulcerative colitis.
Third-degree haemorrhoids prolapse but can be reduced by hand; permanently prolapsed piles are fourth degree. Banding suits first- and second-degree haemorrhoids.
Peutz-Jeghers is autosomal dominant with STK11 mutation on chromosome 19 and mucocutaneous melanosis; polyps are hamartomatous, mainly small bowel.
Amsterdam II requires three relatives with Lynch-related cancers, two successive generations and one case under 50, with FAP excluded.
Pseudocyst fluid cytology shows inflammatory cells, not malignant cells; high amylase and low CEA are typical.
In cystic fibrosis the islets are initially preserved and diabetes is a late complication in older patients, not an early childhood feature.
Motor and vocal tics for over a year with psychosocial impairment indicate Tourette syndrome; an alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine is the usual first drug trial.
Hepatitis B vaccine is safe and IPV is preferred in HIV-infected children; MMR can be given when not severely immunosuppressed, and BCG is not given to HIV-infected children.
India's universal immunisation programme gives PCV at 6 weeks and 14 weeks with a booster at 9 months.
Rabies post-exposure doses are given on days 0, 3, 7 and later, with intervals shorter than four weeks.
Immunoglobulins blunt parenteral live viral vaccines such as measles, mumps and rubella but do not affect oral live vaccines like Ty21a typhoid.
The question asks for the legal category; a minor who commits offences such as assault is legally a juvenile delinquent, while conduct disorder is the psychiatric diagnosis.
India's kala-azar programme uses single-dose IV liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg) as first-line treatment.
The RBSK list of 30 conditions includes Down syndrome (defects), goitre (deficiencies) and rheumatic heart disease (diseases); childhood cancer is not among them.
MUAC of 11.5 to under 12.5 cm without oedema means moderate acute malnutrition, and severe palmar pallor (white palms) means severe anaemia.
Under IMNCI, measles with deep or extensive mouth ulcers is classified as severe complicated measles.
Gasping after initial steps needs bag-and-mask positive pressure ventilation, started with room air in a term neonate.
Early bilious vomiting with distension, multiple air-fluid levels and no distal gas in a stable neonate suggests jejunoileal atresia.
A neonate with oesophageal atresia and fistula is kept nil by mouth on IV fluids with continuous upper-pouch suction, and surgery is not delayed for weight gain.
Pink or brick-dust staining of diapers in the first days of life, with negative dipstick for blood, is due to urate crystals.
Neonatal hypothermia causes hypoglycaemia, hypoxaemia, metabolic acidosis and hyperbilirubinaemia, not metabolic alkalosis.
The Baroda screening test covers only the first 30 months, so it does not suit a 3-year-old, whereas ASQ and Denver II cover him.
The DQ depends on the developmental age of the cube structures shown in the uncaptioned figure, which cannot be seen.
Cyanosis with normal PaO2 but low SpO2 indicates methaemoglobinaemia, a known toxicity of metoclopramide in young children.
Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and coma with a dry mouth point to opioid toxicity, treated with naloxone.

Bilious vomiting within hours of birth points to obstruction distal to the ampulla; of the options only duodenal atresia (double-bubble film) fits, as pyloric stenosis and oesophageal atresia give non-bilious vomiting.
Microcytic anaemia with high ferritin, reticulocytosis and splenomegaly suggests beta-thalassaemia; option D text is garbled.
HIV and hepatitis C are established causes of lymphoid malignancies such as B-cell NHL; hepatitis B is mainly linked to hepatocellular carcinoma.
TRALI occurs within 6 hours and is linked to donor anti-HLA class I/II or anti-neutrophil antibodies; lipids or cytokines can also cause it without antibodies.
Aspirin is antiplatelet, enoxaparin anticoagulant, dabigatran a direct thrombin inhibitor and alteplase thrombolytic.
Croup with stridor at rest and retractions is moderate to severe and needs nebulised adrenaline along with a corticosteroid.
Epileptic spasms in tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, subependymal nodules) respond best to vigabatrin.
Prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, high ferritin, high triglycerides and low fibrinogen meet criteria for haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
Acute pancreatitis (abdominal pain, Cullen sign) during ALL induction is a classic toxicity of L-asparaginase.
Hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia and acute kidney injury after starting therapy for Burkitt lymphoma indicate tumour lysis syndrome, treated with rasburicase.
Donor milk is given voluntarily without payment, donors are screened for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and donor milk lowers NEC but remains inferior to mother's own milk.
Finkelstein test (ulnar deviation with thumb in fist) is positive in de Quervain tenosynovitis.
Schneider first-rank symptoms include third-person auditory hallucinations, thought broadcasting and delusional perception; memory loss is not one.
OCD is diagnosed clinically and treated with SSRIs/clomipramine and CBT (exposure and response prevention); admission is not mandatory.
Purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine substitution is a transition; purine-pyrimidine swap is a transversion, so statement 3 is wrong.
A macule is a small flat coloured lesion not raised above the skin; a larger one is a patch.
Heritable changes from DNA methylation or histone modification without sequence change are epigenetics.
Latrodectism is the syndrome of widow spider (Latrodectus) envenomation with pain, sweating and muscle spasm.
Organophosphate poisoning causes a cholinergic syndrome through AChE inhibition; IV atropine is the treatment, so only statement 3 is correct.
Hookworm causes anaemia, Ascaris Loeffler syndrome, Trichinella myositis; Katayama fever is schistosomiasis, not Loa loa.
In locked-in syndrome a ventral pontine lesion damages both corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts; the cortex is intact and patients answer with eye movements, but the limbs do not move.
Gas gangrene is a clostridial infection of poorly perfused, anaerobic tissue causing a painful, foul wound with gas; radical excision or amputation is often needed.
Diphtheria causes punched-out cutaneous ulcers, laryngeal and pharyngeal symptoms with dysphonia and dysphagia, toxic myocarditis, and bull-neck oedema.
Leishmania donovani is transmitted by the Phlebotomus sandfly.
Casal necklace is the photosensitive neck dermatitis of pellagra, caused by niacin deficiency.
Wickham striae are the fine white lines on lichen planus papules and oral lesions.
Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus, not papillomavirus; the other statements are correct.
Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is scraped off, from exposed dermal papillary capillaries.
CRPS type 1 follows trauma without identifiable nerve injury; type 2 involves nerve damage; Budapest criteria are used for diagnosis.
Osteoporosis is a DXA T-score of -2.5 or lower, so statement 3 is wrong; aortic calcification and spondylosis can falsely raise BMD.
Sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are compatible with pregnancy; methotrexate and leflunomide are teratogenic.
Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder is driven by EBV-infected B cells under immunosuppression.
Exanthem subitum (roseola infantum) is caused by human herpesvirus 6 and, less often, human herpesvirus 7.
Slapped-cheek rash of erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is due to parvovirus B19.
Muttering delirium and coma vigil with picking at bedclothes are classic neuropsychiatric features of typhoid fever.
Necrotising fasciitis types: 1 polymicrobial, 2 group A streptococcal, 3 clostridial/Vibrio, 4 fungal such as Mucorales.
Rapid vancomycin infusion causes histamine release, giving red man syndrome.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome splits the granular layer, so the Nikolsky sign is positive.
Generalised rigidity, trismus, laryngospasm and autonomic instability after an unsterile ear piercing indicate tetanus.
Purulent urethral discharge with gram-negative intracellular diplococci is gonorrhoea.
A slowly advancing serpiginous pruritic track on the foot after beach exposure is cutaneous larva migrans; larva currens moves fast.
GLP-1 (from L cells) and GIP are incretins; GIP comes from duodenal K cells, not M cells.
Exogenous levothyroxine suppresses TSH, raises the T4:T3 ratio and gives low thyroglobulin, which separates it from thyroiditis.
Magnesium deficiency impairs PTH secretion and action, causing hypocalcaemia.
Glargine, detemir and degludec are long-acting analogues; lispro is rapid-acting.
Level 2 hypoglycaemia is glucose below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L), when neuroglycopenic symptoms start and immediate treatment is needed.
Glycyrrhetinic acid in liquorice inhibits 11-beta-HSD2, so cortisol acts on mineralocorticoid receptors (apparent mineralocorticoid excess).
Pegvisomant is the GH receptor antagonist; octreotide, lanreotide and pasireotide are somatostatin analogues.
APS type 2 is commoner and often autosomal dominant; APS type 1 is rare and autosomal recessive (AIRE).
Thyroxine causes weight loss; sulphonylureas, glucocorticoids and beta-blockers cause weight gain. Option D text is garbled.
Teriparatide is recombinant PTH 1-34, an anabolic agent given as a daily subcutaneous injection that stimulates bone formation.
Optic neuritis, Lhermitte sign and ataxia are typical of MS; seizures are uncommon.
In suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a negative CT, a lumbar puncture 12 hours after onset looks for xanthochromia.
Paramyotonia congenita is a sodium channelopathy, malignant hyperthermia a calcium-release (RYR1/CACNA1S) disorder, Thomsen and Becker myotonia chloride channelopathies.
A right frontoparietal lesion causes left hemispatial neglect, so only targets on the right are cancelled; the stem describes the test, so the figure is not needed.
Weakness that spreads ipsilateral arm, ipsilateral leg, contralateral leg, then contralateral arm (around the clock) is typical of a foramen magnum lesion.
Agraphesthesia is inability to recognise numbers or letters traced on the skin; option A describes astereognosis.
MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres) is a mitochondrial encephalomyopathy caused by mtDNA tRNA-Lys mutation.
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome combines multiple seizure types, intellectual impairment and slow spike-and-wave discharges below 3 Hz.
Beta-blockade before alpha-blockade removes beta2 vasodilatation, leaving unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and a hypertensive crisis.
Necrobiosis lipoidica, Charcot joints, exudative maculopathy and acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance) can all be found in diabetic patients.
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and patiromer are gut potassium binders used for hyperkalaemia.
Polystyrene sulfonate resins such as calcium resonium are associated with colonic or intestinal necrosis.
Light chains coprecipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructing tubular casts, i.e. myeloma cast nephropathy.
Fanconi syndrome causes generalised proximal tubular wasting (aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, glycosuria); in myeloma light-chain proteinuria is also present.
Nephronophthisis is autosomal recessive; medullary cystic kidney disease types 1 and 2 and juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy are autosomal dominant.
Uncontrolled hypertension raises the bleeding risk and contraindicates renal biopsy; the others are indications.
Anti-PLA2R antibodies are found in about 70-80% of primary membranous nephropathy.
CKD stage G3a is an eGFR of 45-59 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Refsum disease is phytanic acid accumulation from phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency, causing neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, ataxia and high CSF protein.
Diabetic amyotrophy causes painful, asymmetric proximal lower-limb weakness and wasting with lost knee reflexes.
PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria are diagnostic of Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei).
Hepatitis C spreads through blood; sharing food does not transmit it.
APRI is a validated non-invasive score for liver fibrosis; transaminase levels alone do not predict fibrosis.
Loperamide helps diarrhoea-predominant IBS; lactulose, lubiprostone and sorbitol are used for constipation.
Long-term anthraquinone stimulant laxatives such as senna cause melanosis coli.
A gluten-free diet treats coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis, but not peptic ulcer disease.
The urea breath test and stool antigen test are the non-invasive tests for H. pylori.
In Menetrier disease TGF-alpha excess produces giant fundic folds and protein loss as foveolar mucous cells replace parietal and chief cells, the reverse of statement 3.
Barrett oesophagus is premalignant metaplasia in which squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium in response to reflux.
Krukenberg tumour, Virchow node and Sister Mary Joseph nodule are metastatic signs; Meigs syndrome is a benign ovarian fibroma with ascites and effusion.
Pleural fluid glucose below 60 mg/dL (with pH below 7.2) marks a complicated parapneumonic effusion that needs chest tube drainage.
Severe hypercapnic acidosis with hypoxaemia and rhonchi in a smoker is acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from a COPD exacerbation.
COPD shows reduced FEV1 and PEFR with raised residual volume; diffusion capacity is reduced, not increased, in emphysema.
The anti-IgE antibody omalizumab is used for allergic asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, not idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Silicosis predominantly affects the upper lobes, so statement 1 is wrong; it raises the risk of tuberculosis and fibrosis is related to cumulative dose.
Elderly smoker with clubbing, basal crackles, restrictive spirometry, low DLCO and subpleural honeycombing is the UIP pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Obese snorer with daytime sleepiness has obstructive sleep apnoea; diagnosis is by polysomnography and treatment is CPAP, not a hypnotic.
A therapeutic tap relieves dyspnoea and gives fluid for analysis, and thoracoscopy is used when analysis is inconclusive; medical thoracoscopy is usually done under local anaesthesia with sedation.
A dialysis patient with breathlessness and muffled heart sounds most likely has uraemic pericardial effusion; the stem alone points to it even without seeing the film.
Left-sided blunt trauma with absent breath sounds fits either pneumothorax or traumatic diaphragmatic rupture with bowel herniation; the CT image is needed to decide.
Radio-femoral delay (coarctation), enlarged kidneys (polycystic disease) and buffalo hump (Cushing) point to secondary hypertension; vitiligo does not.
In hypertensive emergency BP is lowered gradually (about 25% in the first hour), not normalised at once, and secondary causes such as renovascular disease are more common, so only statement 1 holds.
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker, telmisartan an ARB, enalapril an ACE inhibitor and eplerenone an aldosterone antagonist.
Takotsubo causes left ventricular apical ballooning, is triggered by emotional stress and mimics STEMI; statements about right ventricular involvement are wrong.

Beta-myosin heavy chain mutations give marked hypertrophy, troponin mutations give fibre disarray with little hypertrophy, and myosin-binding protein C mutations present late with hypertension and arrhythmia.
A tumour plop is an early diastolic sound from a pedunculated left atrial myxoma prolapsing into the mitral orifice.
Flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots define grade 3 retinopathy and are also present in grade 4, which adds papilloedema.
Aschoff bodies are the pathognomonic granulomatous lesions of rheumatic carditis.

In Eisenmenger syndrome a left-to-right shunt reverses to right-to-left (statement 1 is inverted); differential cyanosis of the feet occurs with a PDA, and vasodilators increase right-to-left shunting.
The PDA murmur is a continuous machinery murmur loudest below the left clavicle with late systolic accentuation; it fades when Eisenmenger physiology develops.
Jal Jeevan Mission aims to give every rural household a functional tap connection supplying at least 55 litres per capita per day.
Measles, OPV and yellow fever 17D are live attenuated vaccines; IPV, Hib, hepatitis B and plague vaccines are inactivated or subunit.
In a young infant, not feeding well is a danger sign, so the infant is classified as possible serious bacterial infection / very severe disease, which overrides the local umbilical infection.
Very severe disease in a young infant: give the first dose of IM antibiotics, refer urgently with breastfeeding continued, and give sips of ORS on the way for the dehydration.
The Nischay pregnancy detection kit is supplied to ASHAs and sub-centres for early confirmation of pregnancy.
Pregnancy should be registered as early as possible and within 12 weeks; ASHA is responsible for ensuring early registration, though the ANM formally registers, so 1 and 4 is also arguable.
Under Anemia Mukt Bharat, pregnant women take one IFA tablet daily for at least 180 days starting from the second trimester.
A height below 145 cm makes the pregnancy high risk; age 28 and haemoglobin 11.6 g/dL are not risk criteria.
Pregnant women need about 8 hours of night sleep plus rest after mid-day meals and extra fluids for constipation; only avoiding purgatives like castor oil is correct advice.
In the four-colour triage code, red is highest priority, then yellow, then green (ambulatory), and black (dead or moribund) last.
BMI = 80 / 1.6 squared = 31.25 kg/m2, which falls in WHO obese class I (30 to 34.9).
Long silica exposure with progressive dyspnoea, nodular fibrosis and a snowstorm appearance on chest X-ray is typical of silicosis.
Occupational benzene (benzol) exposure causes leukaemia; aromatic amines like beta-naphthylamine and auramine cause bladder cancer and mineral oil skin cancer.
